prompt: What unit are forces measured in?

options.text: Newtons (N)
Kilograms (kg)
Metres per second (m/s)
Joules (J)

feedback.c: m/s is the unit of speed.

hints: The unit is named after the scientist who wrote the three laws of motion.
solution: Forces are measured in **newtons (N)**, named after Isaac Newton.

prompt: What is the name of the force that acts between two surfaces rubbing together and opposes motion?
hints: It's what lets your shoes grip the ground.
solution: **Friction.** It always acts against the direction of motion between surfaces.

prompt: Mass is measured in [[a]] and weight is measured in [[b]].
hints: Weight is a force.
solution: Mass is measured in **kilograms** (kg). Weight is a force, so it is measured in **newtons** (N).

prompt: Which instrument is used to measure the size of a force?

options.text: A force meter (spring balance)
An electronic balance
A measuring cylinder
A thermometer

feedback.b: An electronic balance is used to find mass in grams or kilograms.
feedback.c: A measuring cylinder measures the volume of a liquid.

hints: It contains a spring that stretches more when the force is bigger.
solution: A **force meter** (spring balance or newton meter) measures force in newtons. The spring stretches further for a bigger force.

prompt: Select **all** the non-contact forces.

options.text: Gravity
Magnetic force
Electrostatic (static electricity) force
Friction
Air resistance
Tension in a rope

hints: Non-contact forces can act across a gap, without the objects touching.
solution: **Gravity, magnetic force and electrostatic force** act without touching. Friction, air resistance and tension are contact forces.

prompt: In a tug of war, the left team pulls with 2,000 N and the right team pulls with 2,000 N. The rope starts still. What happens?

options.text: The rope stays still, because the forces are balanced
The rope moves to the left
The rope moves to the right
The rope moves, because there is 4,000 N of force on it

feedback.b: The pulls are equal, so neither team wins.
feedback.c: The pulls are equal, so neither team wins.
feedback.d: Forces in opposite directions cancel out. The net force is 2,000 − 2,000 = 0 N.

hints: Find the net force: the pulls are in opposite directions.
solution: Net force = 2,000 − 2,000 = **0 N**. The forces are **balanced**, so the rope stays still (Newton's first law).

prompt: A Year 9 student has a mass of 50 kg. What is the student's weight on Earth? Use $g = 10$ N/kg.
hints: Weight = mass × g.
solution: $W = mg = 50 \times 10 = 500$ N

prompt: Match each force to its description.

right.text: The pull of gravity on an object
Drag on an object moving through air
A surface pushing up on an object resting on it
A driving force that pushes an object forwards

hints: Drag is another name for air resistance.
solution: Weight → pull of gravity; friction → opposes motion between surfaces; air resistance → drag in air; support force → a surface pushing up; thrust → driving force forwards.

prompt: What word describes the tendency of an object to resist changes to its motion?
hints: It starts with "i". Objects with more mass have more of it.
solution: **Inertia.** The more mass an object has, the more inertia it has, so the harder it is to speed up, slow down or turn.

prompt: A car with a mass of 1,200 kg accelerates at 3 m/s². What is the net force acting on the car?
hints: Use Newton's second law: $F = ma$.

prompt: A net force of 450 N acts on a quad bike and rider with a total mass of 150 kg. What is their acceleration?
hints: Rearrange $F = ma$ to make $a$ the subject.
solution: $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{450}{150} = 3$ m/s²

prompt: A swimmer pushes the water backwards with her hands. According to Newton's third law, what is the reaction force?

options.text: The water pushes the swimmer forwards
Gravity pulls the swimmer down
The water pushes the swimmer upwards
Water resistance slows the swimmer down

feedback.b: Weight is a different force. A third-law pair is the same type of force, acting between the same two objects.
feedback.c: Upthrust is a real force on the swimmer, but it isn't the reaction to pushing water backwards.
feedback.d: Water resistance is a separate force that opposes her motion.

hints: The reaction is equal in size and opposite in direction to the action.
solution: Action: the swimmer pushes the water **backwards**. Reaction: the water pushes the swimmer **forwards** with an equal force. That's what moves her through the pool.

prompt: An ice hockey puck slides across smooth ice at a **constant velocity**. What can you say about the forces on it?

options.text: They are balanced, so the net force is zero
There must be an unbalanced forward force to keep it moving
There are no forces acting on it at all
The forces are unbalanced, so it moves at a constant speed

feedback.b: A common misconception. Moving objects don't need a forward force to keep going. An unbalanced force would make the puck speed up.
feedback.c: Gravity still pulls it down, and the ice pushes it up. These forces are balanced.
feedback.d: Unbalanced forces change motion. Constant velocity means balanced forces.

hints: Newton's first law: what does a constant velocity tell you about the net force?
solution: Constant velocity means no change in motion, so by Newton's first law the forces are **balanced** (net force = 0). Its weight and the support force from the ice cancel, and there is almost no friction.

prompt: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg on Earth. What happens to her mass and weight when she goes to the Moon?

options.text: Her mass stays 80 kg, but her weight is less
Her mass and her weight are both less
Her mass is less, but her weight stays the same
Her mass and her weight both stay the same

feedback.b: Mass is the amount of matter in her body, which doesn't change when she travels.
feedback.c: It's the other way round: mass stays the same and weight changes.
feedback.d: The Moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's, so her weight changes.

hints: Mass is the amount of matter. Weight is the pull of gravity.
solution: Her **mass stays 80 kg**, because it's the same amount of matter. The Moon's gravity is weaker ($g = 1.6$ N/kg), so her **weight drops** from 800 N to about 128 N.

prompt: Why do passengers lurch forwards when a bus brakes suddenly?

options.text: Their bodies keep moving forwards because of their inertia
The brakes push the passengers forwards
Gravity pulls the passengers forwards
Air in the bus pushes the passengers forwards

feedback.b: The brakes act on the wheels, not on the passengers.
feedback.d: There is no forward push. The passengers simply keep going.

hints: Newton's first law: what does a moving object do if no force acts to stop it?
solution: The bus slows down, but nothing slows the passengers straight away. Because of their **inertia**, they keep moving forwards (Newton's first law) until a seatbelt or seat provides a force to slow them.

prompt: A 900 kg car has a forward driving force of 3,000 N. Friction and air resistance together act backwards with 300 N. What is the car's acceleration?
hints: First find the net force: the forces act in opposite directions.
Then use $a = \dfrac{F}{m}$.
solution: Net force $= 3000 - 300 = 2700$ N forwards. $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{2700}{900} = 3$ m/s²

prompt: A skydiver jumps from a plane. Explain, using forces, why her speed increases at first but then stays constant (terminal velocity).
modelAnswer: When she first jumps, her weight is much bigger than the air resistance, so there is an unbalanced (net) force downwards and she speeds up. As her speed increases, the air resistance on her increases, so the net force gets smaller and she speeds up more slowly. Eventually the air resistance becomes equal to her weight. The forces are then balanced (net force zero), so she stops accelerating and falls at a constant speed. This is terminal velocity.

rubric.criterion: At first, weight is bigger than air resistance, so the net force is downwards and she speeds up
Air resistance increases as her speed increases
When air resistance equals weight, the forces are balanced, so her speed is constant (terminal velocity)

hints: Which force stays the same during the fall, and which one changes?
What does air resistance depend on?
solution: Weight > air resistance → speeds up. Faster → more air resistance. When air resistance = weight → balanced forces → constant speed (**terminal velocity**).

prompt: A Mars rover weighs 1,800 N on Earth, where $g = 10$ N/kg. What would it weigh on Mars, where $g = 3.7$ N/kg?
hints: First find the rover's mass from its Earth weight.
Its mass is the same on Mars. Then use $W = mg$ with the Mars value of $g$.
solution: Mass: $m = \dfrac{W}{g} = \dfrac{1800}{10} = 180$ kg. Weight on Mars: $W = 180 \times 3.7 = 666$ N.

prompt: Select **all** the changes that would **reduce** friction in a bike chain and wheels.

options.text: Oiling the chain
Using ball bearings in the wheel hubs
Making the touching metal parts smoother
Letting the chain get rusty
Pressing the brake pads harder against the wheel

hints: Lubricants and smooth, rolling surfaces reduce friction.
solution: **Oil** (a lubricant), **ball bearings** (rolling instead of sliding) and **smoother surfaces** all reduce friction. Rust makes surfaces rougher, and pressing the brakes harder **increases** friction, which is what brakes are for.

prompt: Use Newton's third law to explain how paddling makes a waka move forwards.
modelAnswer: When the paddlers pull their paddles back through the water, the paddles push the water backwards (action). By Newton's third law, the water pushes the paddles, and so the waka, forwards with an equal and opposite force (reaction). This forward force moves the waka forwards.

rubric.criterion: The paddle pushes the water backwards (action)
The water pushes the paddle/waka forwards with an equal and opposite force (reaction)

hints: Which way does the paddle push the water?
What does the water do back to the paddle?
solution: Paddle pushes water **backwards** → water pushes paddle and waka **forwards** with an equal and opposite force.

prompt: A book rests on a table. The Earth pulls down on the book with a force of 8 N (its weight). Which force forms a **Newton's third law pair** with the book's weight?

options.text: The book pulls the Earth upwards with 8 N
The table pushes the book upwards with 8 N
The book pushes down on the table with 8 N
Friction between the book and the table

feedback.b: This force is equal and opposite, but it acts on the **same** object (the book) and it's a different type of force (a contact force, not gravity). Weight and support are balanced forces, not a third-law pair.
feedback.c: This is the third-law partner of the table's support force, not of the weight.
feedback.d: There's no sideways force, so there is no friction here.

hints: The weight is a gravity force between the Earth and the book.
A third-law pair acts on the two **different** objects involved, and is the same type of force.
solution: The weight is the **Earth pulling the book** by gravity. Its third-law partner is the **book pulling the Earth** upwards by gravity, with the same 8 N. The table's support force is equal and opposite to the weight, but it acts on the same object, so it isn't the pair.

prompt: A 1,500 kg car accelerates steadily from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s. Friction and air resistance total 500 N. What driving force must the engine provide?
hints: First find the acceleration: $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{t}$.
Use $F = ma$ to find the net force, then add the resistance the engine also has to overcome.
solution: Acceleration: $a = \dfrac{20 - 0}{10} = 2$ m/s². Net force needed: $F = ma = 1500 \times 2 = 3000$ N. The engine must also overcome 500 N of resistance, so the driving force $= 3000 + 500 = 3500$ N.

prompt: A skydiver is falling at terminal velocity when she opens her parachute. She slows down, then falls at a new, lower steady speed. Explain why, using forces.
modelAnswer: When the parachute opens, its large area makes the air resistance increase suddenly, so it becomes much bigger than her weight. The net force is now upwards, against her motion, so she decelerates (slows down). She doesn't move upwards, because she is still falling. As her speed decreases, the air resistance decreases. When the air resistance has fallen until it equals her weight again, the forces are balanced, so she falls at a constant, lower speed: a new terminal velocity.

rubric.criterion: Opening the parachute increases air resistance (larger area) so it is bigger than her weight
The net force is upwards, so she slows down
As she slows, air resistance decreases until it equals weight, giving balanced forces and a lower terminal velocity

hints: What does the parachute change: her weight or her air resistance?
As her speed drops, what happens to the air resistance?
solution: Parachute opens → air resistance > weight → net force up → she slows down. Slower → less air resistance → eventually air resistance = weight → balanced → new, lower **terminal velocity**.

prompt: A car travels at a **constant speed** in a straight line along a flat road. What should its free-body diagram show?

options.text: Thrust and drag equal in size; weight and support force equal in size
Thrust bigger than drag; weight and support force equal in size
Only a thrust arrow, because the car is moving forwards
Thrust and drag equal in size, and no vertical forces

feedback.b: If thrust were bigger than drag, the car would speed up.
feedback.c: Drag, weight and the support force still act on a moving car.
feedback.d: Gravity (weight) and the road's support force still act on the car.

hints: Constant speed in a straight line means the forces are balanced.
Don't forget the vertical forces.
solution: Constant velocity means **balanced forces** in both directions: thrust = drag horizontally, and weight = support force vertically. The arrows in each pair should be the same length.

options.text: It is speeding up, because the forces are unbalanced in the forward direction
It is moving at a constant speed, because it is moving forwards

feedback.b: A constant speed needs **balanced** forces. Here the forward force is bigger than the backward force.

stem: Kiri does a bungy jump from a bridge near Queenstown. Her mass is 70 kg. Use $g = 10$ N/kg.
prompt: What is Kiri's weight?
hints: Weight = mass × g.

stem: Kiri does a bungy jump from a bridge near Queenstown. Her mass is 70 kg. Use $g = 10$ N/kg.
prompt: Soon after she jumps, the air resistance on Kiri is 100 N. What is the net force on her at that moment?

options.text: 600 N downwards
800 N downwards
600 N upwards
0 N, because she is falling freely

feedback.b: Air resistance acts **upwards**, against her motion, so subtract it from her weight instead of adding it.
feedback.c: Her weight (700 N) is bigger than the air resistance (100 N), so the net force is downwards.
feedback.d: The forces would only be balanced if the air resistance equalled her weight. Here it is much smaller.

hints: Her weight acts downwards and air resistance acts upwards.
solution: Weight $= 70 \times 10 = 700$ N down. Air resistance = 100 N up. Net force $= 700 - 100 =$ **600 N downwards**, so she is still speeding up.

stem: Kiri does a bungy jump from a bridge near Queenstown. Her mass is 70 kg. Use $g = 10$ N/kg.
prompt: As the bungy cord stretches, it pulls upwards on Kiri. Explain, using forces, why she slows down and stops at the bottom of the jump.
modelAnswer: As the cord stretches, its upward pull (tension) gets bigger and bigger. Once the cord's upward force is bigger than her weight, the forces are unbalanced and the net force on her is upwards. An upward net force on something that is moving downwards makes it slow down, so her speed decreases until she stops at the lowest point.

rubric.criterion: The cord's upward force (tension) increases as it stretches
When the upward force is bigger than her weight, the net force is upwards (unbalanced)
An upward net force while she is moving down makes her slow down until she stops

hints: How does the pull of the cord change as it stretches further?
What does an unbalanced force do to an object's motion?
solution: The key steps are: cord force increases → it becomes bigger than her weight → net force is upwards → she decelerates until she stops. Watch out: at the lowest point she is only still for an instant. The forces are **not** balanced there (the cord pulls up harder than her weight), which is why she is pulled back up again.

stem: Year 9 students launch water rockets on the school field. Each rocket is a plastic bottle, partly filled with water and pumped full of air. When a rocket is released, water is pushed out of the nozzle at the bottom.
prompt: The rocket pushes the water downwards out of the nozzle. According to Newton's third law, what is the reaction force?

options.text: The water pushes the rocket upwards
Gravity pulls the rocket downwards
The air pushes down on the rocket
The ground pushes the water back up

feedback.b: Gravity (weight) is a force between the Earth and the rocket. It isn't the reaction to the rocket pushing the water.
feedback.c: Air resistance acts on the rocket, but it isn't the third-law partner of the rocket pushing the water.
feedback.d: The reaction force acts on the rocket, because the rocket is what pushed the water.

hints: In a third-law pair the two objects swap places: 'A pushes B' becomes 'B pushes A'.
solution: Action: the rocket pushes the water **down**. Reaction: the water pushes the rocket **up**, with a force of the same size. This upward push (thrust) launches the rocket.

stem: Year 9 students launch water rockets on the school field. Each rocket is a plastic bottle, partly filled with water and pumped full of air. When a rocket is released, water is pushed out of the nozzle at the bottom.
prompt: One rocket has a mass of 0.5 kg. At launch, the thrust on it is 20 N upwards. What is its acceleration at launch? Use $g = 10$ N/kg and ignore air resistance.
hints: First find the rocket's weight.
Net force = thrust − weight. Then use $a = \dfrac{F}{m}$.
solution: Weight $= 0.5 \times 10 = 5$ N. Net force $= 20 - 5 = 15$ N upwards. $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{15}{0.5} =$ **30 m/s²**.

stem: Year 9 students launch water rockets on the school field. Each rocket is a plastic bottle, partly filled with water and pumped full of air. When a rocket is released, water is pushed out of the nozzle at the bottom.
prompt: Tane puts much more water in his rocket, which makes it heavier. The thrust at launch is the same as for a lighter rocket. Explain why Tane's rocket has a smaller acceleration.
modelAnswer: His rocket has a bigger mass, so it has more inertia: since $a = F \div m$, the same force gives a bigger mass a smaller acceleration. His rocket also has a bigger weight pulling down, so the net upward force (thrust − weight) is smaller. A smaller net force acting on a bigger mass gives a smaller acceleration.

rubric.criterion: Bigger mass means more inertia / a = F ÷ m, so the same force gives a smaller acceleration
Bigger weight means the net upward force (thrust − weight) is smaller

hints: The extra mass has two effects: one on the net force, and one in $a = \dfrac{F}{m}$.
solution: More mass → more weight, so a smaller net force; and a bigger mass to accelerate. Both make the acceleration smaller.

prompt: What is a force?

options.text: A push or a pull
The energy an object has when it moves
The amount of matter in an object
How fast an object is moving

feedback.b: That is kinetic energy. Energy is measured in joules; forces are measured in newtons.
feedback.c: That is mass, measured in kilograms.
feedback.d: That is speed. A force can **change** how fast something moves.

hints: Think about what you do to open a door or lift a bag.
solution: A **force** is a push or a pull. Forces can change an object's speed, direction or shape, and they are measured in newtons (N).

prompt: What is the name of the non-contact force that pulls objects down towards the Earth?
hints: It is the reason a dropped pen falls to the floor.
solution: **Gravity** pulls objects towards the Earth. The force of gravity on an object is called its weight.

prompt: Forces acting in the same direction [[a]]. Forces acting in opposite directions [[b]]. When the forces on an object are balanced, the net force is [[c]].
hints: Think about two people pushing a car the same way, and then about a tug of war.
solution: Same direction: **add**. Opposite directions: **subtract**. Balanced forces cancel out, so the net force is **zero**.

prompt: Which statement about mass and weight is correct?

options.text: Mass is the amount of matter in an object (kg); weight is the pull of gravity on it (N)
Mass and weight are the same thing, just measured in different units
An object's weight stays the same everywhere, but its mass changes on the Moon
Mass is a force measured in newtons; weight is measured in kilograms

feedback.b: They are different quantities: mass is the amount of matter; weight is a force.
feedback.c: It's the other way round: mass stays the same, but weight changes with the strength of gravity.
feedback.d: The units are swapped. Mass is in kg and weight (a force) is in N.

hints: Which one changes if you go to the Moon?
solution: **Mass** = the amount of matter, in kg; it is the same everywhere. **Weight** = the force of gravity on that mass, in N; it changes with the strength of gravity ($W = mg$).

prompt: Match each example to the Newton's law it best shows.

left.text: Passengers lurch forwards when a bus brakes suddenly

right.text: First law: objects keep moving unless a force acts (inertia)

left.text: A bigger push gives a shopping trolley a bigger acceleration
A swimmer pushes water backwards and the water pushes her forwards

right.text: Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs

hints: Which example is about inertia, which is about F = ma, and which has two objects pushing on each other?
solution: The bus passengers show inertia (first law). The trolley shows that a bigger force gives a bigger acceleration (second law). The swimmer and the water push on each other (third law).

prompt: Friction can be useful, or it can be a nuisance. Select **all** the examples where friction is **useful**.

options.text: Brake pads slowing down a bike wheel
Tyres gripping the road as a car goes round a corner
Rugby boots gripping a muddy field
Striking a match to light it
Friction in a bike chain that has no oil on it
Friction wearing away the soles of your shoes

hints: Useful friction helps you grip, stop or start something. Nuisance friction wears things out or wastes energy.
solution: Useful: brakes, tyre grip, boot grip and striking a match all need friction. A nuisance: a dry bike chain wastes energy as heat, and friction wears out shoe soles.

prompt: Aroha throws a netball with a mass of 0.4 kg. While she is throwing it, the ball accelerates at 50 m/s². What is the net force on the ball while it is being thrown?
hints: Use $F = ma$.

prompt: A net force of 1,800 N gives a loaded trailer an acceleration of 1.2 m/s². What is the mass of the trailer?
hints: Rearrange $F = ma$ to make $m$ the subject.

prompt: Two supermarket trolleys are rolling at the same speed. One is empty and the other is full of groceries. Why is the full trolley harder to stop?

options.text: It has more mass, so it has more inertia
Its weight pushes it forwards
It has less friction on its wheels
It is going faster than the empty trolley

feedback.b: Weight acts **downwards**, not forwards, so it doesn't push the trolley along.
feedback.c: A heavier trolley actually has a little **more** friction, not less. The real reason is its greater mass.
feedback.d: The question says they are rolling at the same speed.

hints: Which property of an object makes it resist changes to its motion?
solution: The full trolley has more **mass**, so it has more **inertia**: it resists changes to its motion more. By $F = ma$, a bigger force is needed to slow it down at the same rate.

prompt: Sam pushes a heavy box across the floor with a force of 50 N. The box slides at a **constant speed**. How big is the friction force on the box?

options.text: Less than 50 N, otherwise the box couldn't move
More than 50 N
0 N, because the box is moving

feedback.b: If friction were less than 50 N, the forces would be unbalanced and the box would speed up. At constant speed the forces are balanced.
feedback.c: If friction were bigger than the push, the box would slow down.
feedback.d: Friction acts whenever surfaces slide over each other. Here it balances Sam's push.

hints: Constant speed means the forces are…?
solution: Constant speed means the forces are **balanced** (Newton's first law), so friction must equal the push: **50 N**. A push bigger than friction is only needed to **speed up** the box.

prompt: Use Newton's first law to explain why passengers in a car need to wear seatbelts.
modelAnswer: Newton's first law says an object keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction unless an unbalanced force acts on it. If a car stops suddenly in a crash, the passengers keep moving forwards at the car's original speed, because of their inertia. Without a seatbelt, nothing stops them until they hit the dashboard, the windscreen or the seat in front. A seatbelt provides the backward force that slows them down with the car, so they don't hit anything.

rubric.criterion: States or uses the first law: objects keep moving (inertia) unless an unbalanced force acts
When the car stops suddenly, the passengers keep moving forwards
The seatbelt provides the (backward) force to slow the passengers down with the car, so they don't hit the inside of the car

hints: What happens to a passenger's body when the car suddenly stops?
What force could slow the passenger down?
solution: Inertia keeps the passenger moving when the car stops. The seatbelt supplies the unbalanced force needed to slow them down safely.

prompt: Hemi says, "My weight is 60 kg." Explain what is wrong with his statement, and work out his actual weight. Use $g = 10$ N/kg.
modelAnswer: 60 kg is Hemi's mass: the amount of matter in his body. Weight is a force (the pull of gravity on his mass), so it is measured in newtons, not kilograms. His weight is $W = mg = 60 \times 10 = 600$ N.

rubric.criterion: Explains that 60 kg is his mass (amount of matter), while weight is a force measured in newtons

hints: What unit are forces measured in?
solution: Mass is in kilograms; weight is a force in newtons. $W = 60 \times 10 = 600$ N.

prompt: Select **all** the pairs of forces that are Newton's third law (action–reaction) pairs.

options.text: The Earth pulls an apple down; the apple pulls the Earth up
Your foot pushes the ground backwards; the ground pushes your foot forwards
A book's weight pulls it down; the table's support force pushes the book up
A rocket pushes hot gases down; the gases push the rocket up
A car's thrust pushes it forwards; air resistance pushes it backwards
A magnet pulls on a paper clip; the paper clip pulls on the magnet

hints: In a third-law pair, the two forces act on **different** objects and are the same type of force.
solution: Third-law pairs act on two different objects: Earth and apple, foot and ground, rocket and gases, magnet and paper clip. The book's weight and the support force both act on the book (and are different types of force), and the car's thrust and air resistance both act on the car. Those are forces on one object, not third-law pairs.

prompt: Mere has a mass of 60 kg and her bike has a mass of 10 kg. She pedals with a driving force of 280 N. Friction and air resistance together are 70 N. What is her acceleration?
hints: Find the net force first.
Use the total mass of Mere and her bike.
solution: Net force $= 280 - 70 = 210$ N. Total mass $= 60 + 10 = 70$ kg. $a = \dfrac{F}{m} = \dfrac{210}{70} =$ **3 m/s²**.

prompt: A lift (elevator) carries people upwards at a **constant speed**. How does the upward pull of the cable compare with the total weight of the lift and the people?

options.text: They are equal, because the lift is moving at a constant velocity
The pull is bigger, because the lift is moving upwards
The pull is smaller, otherwise the lift would speed up
There is no weight, because the lift is moving upwards

feedback.b: A bigger upward pull is only needed to **speed up**. Once it's moving steadily, the forces are balanced (Newton's first law).
feedback.c: If the pull were smaller than the weight, there would be a downward net force and the lift would slow down.
feedback.d: Gravity acts on the lift and the people all the time, whichever way they're moving.

hints: Constant speed in a straight line means the forces are…?
Moving upwards doesn't mean the upward force has to be bigger.
solution: At a constant velocity the forces are **balanced**, so the cable's pull equals the total weight. The pull is only bigger than the weight while the lift is speeding up at the start of the trip.

prompt: A car with a mass of 1,000 kg is travelling at 20 m/s. The driver brakes and the car stops in 4 s. What is the size of the net braking force on the car?
hints: First find the car's acceleration: change in velocity ÷ time.
Then use $F = ma$. (You only need the size, so ignore the minus sign.)
solution: $a = \dfrac{0 - 20}{4} = -5$ m/s² (slowing down). $F = ma = 1000 \times 5 =$ **5,000 N**, acting backwards.
